source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 2 (printed page 11): Table 2.1 (characteristics of the five kingdoms), Whittaker's Five Kingdom Classification, the three-domain system, and the start of the discussion of earlier classification systems.

questions.question: Who proposed the Five Kingdom Classification?
questions.explanation: The page states that R.H. Whittaker proposed the Five Kingdom Classification.
questions.source_text: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed a Five Kingdom Classification.

questions.question: In which year was the Five Kingdom Classification proposed by Whittaker?
questions.explanation: The page gives 1969 for Whittaker's proposal.
questions.source_text: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed a Five Kingdom Classification.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the five kingdoms named by Whittaker?
questions.explanation: The five kingdoms named were Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
questions.source_text: The kingdoms defined by him were named Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

questions.question: Which criteria did Whittaker mainly use for his classification?
questions.explanation: The page lists cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.
questions.source_text: The main criteria for classification used by him include cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships.

questions.question: The three-domain system divides which kingdom into two domains?
questions.explanation: The three-domain system splits Monera into two domains and leaves the eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain.
questions.source_text: divides the Kingdom Monera into two domains, leaving the remaining eukaryotic kingdoms in the third domain

questions.question: The three-domain proposal leads to how many kingdoms in total, as described on this page?
questions.explanation: The page says the three-domain system gives a six kingdom classification.
questions.source_text: in the third domain and thereby a six kingdom classification.

questions.question: Which kingdom in Table 2.1 has prokaryotic cells with no nuclear membrane?
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 lists Monera as prokaryotic with the nuclear membrane absent; the other four kingdoms are eukaryotic with a nuclear membrane present.
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Cell type - Monera: Prokaryotic; Nuclear membrane - Monera: Absent

questions.question: Match each kingdom with its cell wall as given in Table 2.1.
questions.explanation: Table 2.1: Monera noncellulosic (polysaccharide + amino acid), Fungi with chitin, Plantae cellulose, Animalia absent.
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Cell wall - Monera: Noncellulosic (Polysaccharide + amino acid); Fungi: Present with chitin; Plantae: Present (cellulose); Animalia: Absent

questions.question: According to Table 2.1, the cell wall in Kingdom Protista is:
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 gives 'Present in some' for the cell wall of Protista.
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Cell wall - Protista: Present in some

questions.question: According to Table 2.1, the body organisation of Kingdom Fungi is:
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 gives multicellular/loose tissue for Fungi. Cellular is given for Monera and Protista.
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Body organisation - Fungi: Multiceullar/loose tissue

questions.question: Which kingdom has the tissue/organ/organ system level of body organisation in Table 2.1?
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 gives tissue/organ/organ system for Animalia and tissue/organ for Plantae.
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Body organisation - Plantae: Tissue/organ; Animalia: Tissue/organ/organ system

questions.question: According to Table 2.1, which kingdom includes chemosynthetic and photosynthetic autotrophs as well as heterotrophs?
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 lists Monera as autotrophic (chemosynthetic and photosynthetic) and heterotrophic (saprophytic/parasitic).
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Mode of nutrition - Monera: Autotrophic (chemosynthetic and photosynthetic) and Heterotrophic (saprophytic/parasitic)

questions.question: According to Table 2.1, the mode of nutrition of Kingdom Fungi is:
questions.explanation: Table 2.1 lists Fungi as heterotrophic, saprophytic or parasitic. Holozoic is listed for Animalia.
questions.source_text: Table 2.1: Mode of nutrition - Fungi: Heterotrophic (Saprophytic/Parasitic); Animalia: Heterotrophic (Holozoic/Saprophytic etc.)

questions.question: In the earlier classification, the character that unified all organisms placed under 'Plants' was:
questions.explanation: The page says all organisms in that kingdom had a cell wall, which placed together groups that differed widely in other characteristics.
questions.source_text: The character that unified this whole kingdom was that all the organisms included had a cell wall in their cells.

questions.question: Which of the following were included under 'Plants' in earlier classification systems?
questions.explanation: The page lists bacteria, blue green algae, fungi, mosses, ferns, gymnosperms and angiosperms. Insects are not mentioned.
questions.source_text: Earlier classification systems included bacteria, blue green algae, fungi, mosses, ferns, gymnosperms and the angiosperms under

questions.question: Chlamydomonas and Spirogyra are cited as an example of the earlier grouping of:
options: Unicellular and multicellular organisms together under algae
questions.explanation: The page says the earlier system grouped unicellular and multicellular organisms together, for example Chlamydomonas and Spirogyra under algae.
questions.source_text: It also grouped together the unicellular organisms and the multicellular ones, say, for example, Chlamydomonas and Spirogyra were placed together under algae.

questions.question: The earlier classification did not differentiate between which two groups, despite their different wall composition?
options: Heterotrophic fungi and autotrophic green plants
questions.explanation: The page says the system did not differentiate the heterotrophic fungi from the autotrophic green plants.
questions.source_text: The classification did not differentiate between the heterotrophic group – fungi, and the autotrophic green plants

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The earlier 'Plants' category brought together prokaryotic bacteria and cyanobacteria with eukaryotic groups.
Reason (R): All the organisms in that category were unified by the presence of a cell wall.
options: Both A and R are true, and R correctly explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.explanation: Because the unifying character was just a cell wall, groups that were widely different, including prokaryotes and eukaryotes, were placed together.
questions.source_text: This placed together groups which widely differed in other characteristics. It brought together the prokaryotic bacteria and the blue green algae (cyanobacteria) with other groups which were eukaryotic.
